title: Before and After Puzzle
statement:
Each string in `phrases` is a phrase: one or more words of lowercase letters, separated by single spaces, with no space at either end.

Two phrases can be joined when the **last** word of the first one is the **same word** as the **first** word of the second one. Joining writes the first phrase followed by the rest of the second phrase, so the shared word appears only once (`"writing code"` and `"code rocks"` join into `"writing code rocks"`).

Consider every ordered pair `phrases[i]`, `phrases[j]` with `i != j` (both orders count, and two equal phrases at different positions may be joined). Return all the different joined phrases, sorted in lexicographic order. Return an empty list when no pair can be joined.
constraints: phrases[i] contains only lowercase English letters and spaces
No phrase starts or ends with a space, and no phrase has two spaces in a row

examples.name: Example 2
input: a chip off the old block
expected: a chip off the old block party
a man on a mission impossible
a man on a mission statement
a quick bite to eat my words

notes:
## Intuition

The direct way tries every ordered pair of phrases, splits both into words and compares the last word of one with the first word of the other: O(n²) pairs, each costing O(L) to split. Better: a phrase can only follow phrases ending in its own first word, so index the phrases by their first word once, and each phrase looks up exactly the partners that fit.

## Approach

1. Build `startsWith`: a map from each first word to the indices of the phrases that begin with it.
2. For each phrase `i`, take its `last` word and fetch the `partners` that start with that word.
3. Skip `j === i` (a phrase cannot join itself, though an equal phrase elsewhere can).
4. The partner begins with `last`, so `phrases[j].slice(last.length)` is everything after the shared word (empty or starting with a space). Append it to `phrases[i]` and add the result to the set `puzzles`, which removes repeats.
5. Return the set's contents sorted.

## Example 1, step by step

`startsWith` maps `"writing" -> [0]` and `"code" -> [1]`. Phrase 0 ends in `"code"`, whose partners are `[1]`; `rest` is `" rocks"`, giving `"writing code rocks"`. Phrase 1 ends in `"rocks"`, which starts no phrase. The answer is `["writing code rocks"]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n·L + P·L + P log P · L), where n is the number of phrases, L their length and P the number of joined phrases (at most n², and each is at most 2L long).
- Space: O(n·L + P·L) for the map and the set of results.

## Pitfalls

- Compare whole words, not prefixes: `"x ab"` must not join `"a y"`, and `"aa a"` ends in `"a"`, not `"aa"`.
- Write the shared word once: `"a"` joined with `"a"` (at different positions) is `"a"`, not `"a a"`.
- Both orders count, so `"ab ba"` and `"ba ab"` give two different results.
- The same text can come from different pairs; keep it once.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `startsWith` | first word to the list of phrase indices beginning with it |
| `first`, `last` | the first word of a phrase, and the last word of phrase `i` |
| `words` | phrase `i` split into words |
| `partners` | indices of phrases that can follow phrase `i` |
| `rest` | the partner phrase without its first word |
| `puzzles` | the distinct joined phrases |

narration.2: Index the phrases by their first word so partners can be found without trying every pair.
narration.4: The first word is everything before the first space.
narration.5: Is this the first phrase seen with that first word?
narration.6: Then start an empty list of indices for it.
narration.8: Record that phrase i begins with this word.
narration.11: A set keeps each joined phrase only once.
narration.13: Split phrase i into its words...
narration.14: ...and take the last one, which the next phrase must start with.
narration.15: These are the phrases that begin with that word (none if the word starts no phrase).
narration.16: Try each partner j in turn.
narration.17: A phrase may not be joined to itself (an equal phrase at another index is fine).
narration.20: The partner starts with the shared word, so cutting that many characters leaves the rest of it.
narration.21: Write phrase i, then the partner's remaining words, and keep the result.
narration.24: Return the distinct joined phrases in lexicographic order.
